questions.knowledge_point: Calculating Limits of Multivariable Rational Functions by Factoring
questions.worked_solution:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ as follows: 

$$
{lim}_{(x,y)\to (1,2)}\frac{2{x}^{2}+3xy-2{y}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}-xy}=\frac{2\cdot {1}^{2}+3\cdot 1\cdot 2-2\cdot {2}^{2}}{2\cdot {1}^{2}-1\cdot 2}=\frac{0}{0}
$$

However, we can simplify the limit by first factoring the denominator, and then canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{(x,y)\to (1,2)}\frac{2{x}^{2}+3xy-2{y}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}-xy} & ={lim}_{(x,y)\to (1,2)}\frac{2{x}^{2}+4xy-xy-2{y}^{2}}{x(2x-y)} \\  & ={lim}_{(x,y)\to (1,2)}\frac{2x(x+2y)-y(x+2y)}{x(2x-y)} \\  & ={lim}_{(x,y)\to (1,2)}\frac{(2x-y)(x+2y)}{x(2x-y)} \\  & ={lim}_{(x,y)\to (1,2)}\frac{x+2y}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{(x,y)\to (1,2)}\frac{x+2y}{x} & =\frac{1+2\cdot 2}{1} \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the limit evaluates to $5.$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating Limits Along Different Paths for Multivariable Functions
questions.problem:
Which of the following statements are true regarding the limit given below?

$$
{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\,\frac{2{x}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}-y}
$$

- The limit evaluates to $0$ along the path $y=x$
- The limit evaluates to $2$ along the path $y={x}^{2}$
- The limit exists and is equal to $2$
questions.worked_solution:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}:$

$$
{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\,\frac{2{x}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}-y}=\frac{2\cdot {0}^{2}}{2\cdot {0}^{2}-0}=\frac{0}{0}
$$

However, the function cannot be simplified by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

We attempt to evaluate the limit by approaching $(0,0)$ from different paths.

- Statement I is true. Taking $x\to (0,0)$ along the path $y=x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,y=x}\,\frac{2{x}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}-y} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{2{x}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}-x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{2{x}^{2}}{x(2x-1)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{2x}{2x-1} \\  & =\frac{2\cdot 0}{2\cdot 0-1} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is also true. Taking $x\to (0,0)$ along the path $y={x}^{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,y={x}^{2}}\,\frac{2{x}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}-y} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{2{x}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}-{x}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{2{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\,2 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. Because the limit evaluates to different results on two different paths, we conclude that the limit does not exist:

$$
{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\,\frac{2{x}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}-y}=\text{DNE}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating Limits of Multivariable Rational Functions by Factoring
questions.worked_solution:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (-1,-1)}\frac{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}-xy} & =\frac{(-1)^{2}-(-1)^{2}}{(-1)^{2}-(-1)(-1)} \\  & =\frac{1-1}{1-1} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

However, we can simplify the limit by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (-1,-1)}\frac{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}-xy} & ={lim}_{x\to (-1,-1)}\frac{(x+y)(x-y)}{x(x-y)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (-1,-1)}\frac{(x+y)\cancel{(x-y)}}{x\cancel{(x-y)}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (-1,-1)}\frac{x+y}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it using direct substitution:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (-1,-1)}\frac{x+y}{x} & =\frac{-1+(-1)}{(-1)} \\  & =\frac{(-2)}{(-1)} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the limit evaluates to $2.$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating Limits of Multivariable Functions Using Conjugate Multiplication
questions.worked_solution:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\frac{\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{y}+x-y}{\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{y}} & =\frac{\sqrt{0}-\sqrt{0}+0-0}{\sqrt{0}-\sqrt{0}} \\  & =\frac{0-0+0-0}{0-0} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

However, we can simplify the limit by first multiplying the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\frac{\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{y}+x-y}{\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{y}} & ={lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\frac{(\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{y}+x-y)(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y})}{(\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{y})(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\frac{(\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{y})(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y})+(x-y)(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y})}{x-y} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\frac{x-y+(x-y)(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y})}{x-y} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\frac{(x-y)(1+\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y})}{x-y} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\frac{\cancel{(x-y)}(1+\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y})}{\cancel{x-y}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (0,0)}(1+\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y})\end{aligned}
$$

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}(1+\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}) & =1+\sqrt{0}+\sqrt{0} \\  & =1+0+0 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the limit evaluates to $1.$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating Limits of Multivariable Functions Using Conjugate Multiplication
questions.worked_solution:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\frac{\sqrt{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+9}-3}{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}} & =\frac{\sqrt{({0}^{2})({0}^{2})+9}-3}{({0}^{2})({0}^{2})} \\  & =\frac{3-3}{0} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

However, we can simplify the limit by first multiplying the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the numerator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\frac{\sqrt{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+9}-3}{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}} & ={lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\frac{(\sqrt{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+9}-3)(\sqrt{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+9}+3)}{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+9}+3)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\frac{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+9-9}{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+9}+3)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\frac{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+9}+3)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\frac{\cancel{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}}{\cancel{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+9}+3)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+9}+3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+9}+3} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{({0}^{2})({0}^{2})+9}+3} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{9}+3} \\  & =\frac{1}{3+3} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the limit evaluates to $\frac{1}{6}.$
